doc.title: Lexical
doc.paragraph: The Lexical analyzer for Adaptive Framework is responsible for tokenizing Adaptive Scripts, Templates and Expressions as inputs for the parser. In this section, we will cover comments and whitespace, identifiers, keywords, operators, and literals.

Identifiers are sequences of characters that are used to identify a variable name, category, function name, method name, parameter name, qualifier name symbol reference, interface name, type variable name, or object property name.
Identifiers have no length limit and are case-sensitive.
doc.code: Identifier ::= IdentifierStart IdentifierContinue* IdentifierStart ::= ID_START | '$' | '_' IdentifierContinue ::= ID_CONTINUE | '$' | ZWNJ | ZWJ

list.item: ID_START is any codepoint with ID_START flag
ID_CONTINUE is any codepoint with ID_CONTINUE flag

doc.paragraph: Separately, the lexical analyzer recognizes pound_identifier tokens: a leading # followed by an identifier-like name (for example #block or #compile). You may see them in decompile output; they are not ordinary identifiers and cannot be used as variable names. Most are not something you write in normal scripts (see Language Features); policy forms such as #compile are the exception.
When declaring a variable name, you may use any identifier with the exception of the following reserved names:
doc.code: false INF Infinity NaN null true undefined break case catch const continue default do else extends finally for function if interface let return switch throw try type void while as async await class delete export from import in instanceof super this typeof var with
doc.paragraph: Literals are constant that can be used as a values inside expressions. There are three types of literals:
A Array Literal is a sequence of literals, separated by , and enclosed in [ and ].
An Object Literal is a sequence of Identifier : Literal pairs, separated by , and enclosed by { and }.
A Scalar Literal may be one of: Double, Integer, String, true, false or null.

A regular expression literal is written as in ECMAScript, where a value can start: /pattern/flags. Its value has data type regexp and is compiled once, when the script is compiled, so a pattern that does not compile is a syntax error at the literal. The pattern is passed to the regular expression engine as written: backslashes are not doubled. Write a / in the pattern as \/ or inside a class ([/]). After a value, / divides, and /= always divides and assigns.
The typed literal "a+b"re (or "a+b"regexp) is the same value, written as a string, so its backslashes are doubled: "\\d+"re is /\d+/.

Patterns use ICU regular expression syntax, which is close to ECMAScript and Perl: classes such as \d and \p{L}, groups, named groups (?<name>...), lookahead and lookbehind, and lazy quantifiers. A pattern matches anywhere in the value unless ^ and $ anchor it: regexp_match("xaab", /a+b/) is true and regexp_match("xaab", /^a+b$/) is false.
Flags follow the closing /:

list.item: m lets ^ and $ match at the start and end of each line.
s lets . match a line terminator.
x ignores whitespace and # comments in the pattern.
u is accepted and changes nothing: patterns are always Unicode.

doc.paragraph: The regexp functions take a regexp, not a string: regexp_match(value, regexp), regexp_index_of(value, regexp) (the code point index of the first match, or -1), and regexp_replace(value, regexp, replacement, limit?) (limit 1 by default, -1 for every match). In the replacement, $1 is the text of group 1, $0 the whole match, ${name} a named group, and a backslash makes the next character literal (\$). To use a pattern you have as a string, convert it once with to_regexp(s) and keep the result; a regexp value read from data is compiled each time a function uses it, unless you compile it with compile<regexp>(r).

A pattern that backtracks without bound on a value (for example /^(a+)+$/ on a long run of a that does not end the way it expects) stops with a payload_too_large error after about a tenth of a second of backtracking.
